newsitem.title: CHINA: China road firms eye foreign listings, investment.
newsitem.headline: China road firms eye foreign listings, investment.

text.p: Foreign listings are just around the corner for several Chinese highway companies, an official said on Friday, adding that China needed $6.5 billion in foreign money to build up its overstretched road network.

Shenzhen Expressway Company Ltd in southern Guangdong province was among the first, planning to place H shares, or mainland Chinese shares listed in Hong Kong, in the first quarter of 1997, a company official said by telephone.
He declined to give details, saying the firm was still waiting for government approval.

Zhang Wensheng, director of the Ministry of Communications' Restructuring Economic System and Legislation Department, said plans for Shenzhen Expressway to list last October had been put off because the market was not favourable.
Beijing gave Shenzhen Expressway approval earlier this year to list 510 million H shares to raise HK$1.0-1.5 billion ($128.2-$192.3 million), Hong Kong media has reported.
Merrill Lynch was expected to be the lead underwriter.

Several other highway development companies, including Chengyu Expressway Co in southwestern Sichuan province, Huning Expressway Co in central Jiangsu province and Huhangrong Expressway Co in the eastern coastal province of Zhejiang were applying for foreign listings, Zhang said.
He declined to give details on the planned listings and company officials could not be reached for comment.
China needs $65 billion for highway construction in the next five years and hopes to raise 10 percent of that, or $6.5 billion, from abroad, Zhang said.
He did not say how much of that would come from overseas listings.
"We expect a very large deficit in highway construction," Zhang said in a telephone interview, adding that the ministry expected a 15 to 25 percent shortfall in funding.
Existing financial sources would not increase in the short term and China badly needed new funding channels, officials have said.

China felt confident about inviting foreigners to invest in highway construction because overseas businesses had already bought shares and management rights from a number of local highway companies, Zhang said.
"By welcoming foreign investment, we get money as well as management and technical expertise," Zhang said.
Asked about the risk of slow returns, he said most companies to be listed already had completed highways on their books.

Hainan Kaili Development and Construction Co Ltd was financing a 5.4 billion yuan expressway in the southern island province by selling shares to foreign shareholders, a company official said this month but gave no details.

Toll operator Anhui Expressway Co Ltd raised HK$872.6 million when it made its debut on the Hong Kong bourse last October, the Xinhua news agency said. The company was the first Chinese highway to list overseas.
The Anhui company would buy operating rights on a road linking the northern port of Shanhaiguan with Guangzhou, capital of southern Guangdong province, in January 1997, it said.

Authorities in central Anhui planned to build 5,000 km (3,107 miles) of roads, including 650 km (404 miles) of highways, in the next five years at a projected cost of 20 billion yuan ($2.4 billion), it said.
The provincial government had hoped to attract foreign investment, but won little interest, Xinhua said.
"China's economy is booming, and with it you will see highways springing up," Zhang said.
